title: From Athlete to AI: Summize CEO's Legal Tech Entrepreneurial Journey (Tom Dunlop)
author: Tom Dunlop

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Dunlop does not assess legal-specific AI workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration or verified copilots. Instead, he frames legal-services innovation around comparison-site transparency and potential commoditisation by quality and price, offering a materially different market mechanism rather than supporting or rejecting the cluster’s software thesis.
qs: The whole concept was really, can legal services be a bit more commoditized based on quality and price, and can you do that at scale?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Dunlop accepts the cluster’s workflow-redesign premise and adds a concrete implementation model: structure contract data in a system of record while delivering AI assistance inside familiar tools rather than through disruptive standalone interfaces. His gradual voice-driven automation prediction extends this toward bounded contract execution, although the source does not substantively address verification, user expertise or broader organisational outcomes.
qs: And I think the background processes, the data storage, being that system of record, essentially categorizing the data is important, that we have quality data and it's structured in the right way, is obviously all within Summize.
The simplest thing is to keep it outlook word and then that's it.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Dunlop supports the cluster’s account of extending legal AI beyond isolated drafting into embedded, connected workflows that reduce application-switching and may gradually enable delegated contract tasks. His contribution is limited to workflow integration and a speculative voice-driven future; it does not address autonomy levels, error propagation or verification bottlenecks.
qs: Then you're taking them away from that to go and do another action that is in a particular.com, then log in and get used to the UI, and then you've got to go back to the document again.
I think you can see the gradual move towards that.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Dunlop directly supports the cluster’s core claim that dependable legal AI requires more than standalone model output: contract data must be curated, AI layered onto organised information, and outputs informed by company-specific risks and context. His product-experience account does not establish broader agentic autonomy or reliability through measured results.
qs: We believe that there's still a huge requirement for almost this curation of the data, which is what we do as step one, and then we overlay that gen AI on the top.
AI on its own is not going to flag that necessarily as being a huge risk because it doesn't necessarily recognize that for that brand it's a big risk.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: Dunlop exemplifies the cluster’s distinction between pragmatic product positioning and unproven transformation: he explicitly treats embedded chat and voice as an assumption about future work and describes autonomous NDA creation as a hypothetical possibility, not a demonstrated capability.
qs: So we're almost going with that direction and assuming that that's the future of work.

So yeah, could I see a world where someone essentially does a voice note and says, create an NDA that has these properties and it then goes away and it might ask you some more questions, but ultimately it's an autonomous process.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports the proposition through two operational routes: embedded business self-service that reduces work reaching legal, and technology-enabled outsourced delivery with human oversight. It provides concrete workflow mechanisms but no measured results or evidence that released capacity was actually converted into strategic work.
qs: I like to think of this about reducing the volume that gets into legal.
Our team of legal professionals leveraged tech and project management principles with the right amount of human oversight to deliver precise, efficient and cost-effective legal solutions.

kp.k: Manual contract diligence motivated automated summarization
kp.d: Dunlop traces Summize's origins to his in-house experience reviewing hundreds of contracts and repeatedly extracting the same information, a process he says took months. He dates the initial technical work to approximately 2018. This is a founder's account of a task-level automation opportunity, not a measured study of productivity gains.
qs: I was going through a due diligence process, reviewing hundreds of contracts at the time, trying to pull out the same information, really manual, took me months.
This was more like 2018.

kp.k: Business self-service aims to reduce legal intake
kp.d: Dunlop describes enabling business users to create contracts without legal involvement and submit review requests through existing applications, including Teams, Slack, Outlook, Gmail, Salesforce and HubSpot. He presents this as a means of making business users more self-sufficient and reducing the volume reaching in-house legal teams; the transcript supplies no quantified reduction.
qs: So a big part of our products actually is about allowing the business to be a lot more self-sufficient.
They can create contracts without legal involvement and they can submit and get in triage without actually going to a different platform.
That's the first use case is reducing the volume that gets into legal and making the business more self-sufficient.

kp.k: Word-based AI supports lawyers reviewing remaining contracts
kp.d: For work that still reaches legal, Dunlop describes an augmentation model centered on a Microsoft Word add-in. Its stated functions include summarization, playbook access, an AI assistant, released AI redlining, and workflow coordination. These are vendor-described capabilities intended to improve lawyer efficiency, rather than evidence of lawyer replacement or demonstrated time savings.
qs: We do that through a word add-in primarily because most lawyers want to stay in Microsoft Word and believe it's a good word processor or word editor.
That can be summarization, playbook access, an AI assistant. We've got AI redlining that we've released, and also just general workflow and tasks and conversations to be accessible via Word.

kp.k: Contract summaries reduce dependence on legal interpretation
kp.d: Dunlop says post-signature natural-language summaries allow business users to understand contracts without a lawyer explaining them. He also describes querying extracted information through familiar applications, including compound questions about renewal dates, notice periods and automatic renewal across contracts with a particular entity. These are claims about product functionality and business-user independence, not independently evaluated comprehension or accuracy findings.
qs: we provide a really natural language, kind of detail rich summary of a contract that a business user could look at, they completely understand out of the box.
Again, without having that almost like legal translator sat there explaining what a contract might be saying.
out of all my contracts with particular entity with Google, when do they renew and what notice period would I have to provide? And if I don't, does it auto-renew?

kp.k: Generative AI complements earlier extraction and relevance techniques
kp.d: Dunlop describes the original system as combining pattern recognition, entity extraction and proprietary relevance algorithms. Producing useful natural-language output from extracted information was initially difficult; generative AI subsequently helped fill that gap. His account positions generative AI as a layer over curated contract data, rather than a wholesale replacement of the earlier system.
qs: So we used elements of AI back then, which was more to do with the pattern recognition, entity extraction, a number of different AI models.
But a lot of it actually was algorithm-based on our side that we developed based on relevance.
We believe that there's still a huge requirement for almost this curation of the data, which is what we do as step one, and then we overlay that gen AI on the top.

kp.k: Company-specific risk limits generic AI contract analysis
kp.d: Dunlop argues that AI can produce superficially impressive output yet struggle with long, unstructured contracts and company-specific priorities. His example is an IP restriction affecting logo use that matters particularly to a brand-conscious company. He says customer templates, rules and configurable prompts help establish relevance, while acknowledging that generative AI may eventually perform more of this initial complex reasoning.
qs: if you've got really unstructured data that's quite a long document, which most contracts are, AI still struggles to give a good output.
AI on its own is not going to flag that necessarily as being a huge risk because it doesn't necessarily recognize that for that brand it's a big risk.
It might be that we just take their template and their precedent template and create a bunch of rules that are developed from that, which can feed the engine which finds relevance.
but do I see a world where gen AI starts to do more of that complex reasoning at the start, probably.

kp.k: Workflow integration becomes the vendor's principal differentiator
kp.d: Dunlop says embedded workflows have become more important to Summize's competitive positioning than summarization as generative AI capabilities expand. He argues that forcing users to leave their existing document workflow, log into a separate platform and learn its interface creates friction and may undermine efficiency. His proposed response is to connect contract touchpoints across existing tools.
qs: we've realized the importance of being embedded in people's tools is actually the real USP that we have.

But as I say, a lot of our stuff now is actually linking together, we call it a digital thread, but linking together the full experience of touch points for contracts, through all these different tools, with a load of the smarts built in, like the summarization elements.
It's actually not necessarily creating efficiencies. It's a diversion from what they want to do.

kp.k: Embedded access still depends on a centralized contract repository
kp.d: Dunlop distinguishes the user interface from the underlying system of record. Summize seeks to retain extracted, structured contract data in its own repository even when users interact through other applications. He describes Google Drive and SharePoint integrations primarily as outward document transfers or backups, with querying centered on Summize's extracted data.
qs: We typically provide it more one way as in we want Summize to be the core repository and the reason for that is obviously that we extract all this data and we want people to be querying the data from Summize rather than through G-Drive or SharePoint, they don't have the functionality.
We can push documents that we store in Summize into a G-Drive folder almost as a backup or a SharePoint folder.

the background processes, the data storage, being that system of record, essentially categorizing the data is important, that we have quality data and it's structured in the right way, is obviously all within Summize.

kp.k: Customer comfort determines the extent of contract automation
kp.d: Dunlop reports that some customers already automate NDA creation in Slack, dispatch through DocuSign, return of the executed document, filing and summarization. He contrasts that route with negotiated contracts sent for signature by pressing a button. The claimed automation is conditional on customer preferences and does not establish autonomous handling of all contract work.
qs: We do have a number of customers that, let's say in Slack, they create an NDA and they actually are comfortable. They want to send that straight to DocuSign.
The moment it's signed by both parties, it goes back into Summize into a dedicated folder. We summarize it and it's done, all automated.
depending on how the customer wants to work.

kp.k: Roadmap extends embedded workflows and AI task complexity
kp.d: Dunlop identifies increasing AI task complexity across the product over the next 12 months and deeper native integrations over the next few months as roadmap priorities, measured relative to the interview. He envisages lawyers handling requests, review, conversations and signature through Word and Outlook without visiting Summize's website. He links greater autonomy to what users are comfortable allowing AI to handle; this is a development direction rather than a completed deployment claim.
qs: rather than single task completion, is just getting more sophisticated with AI usage.
That is something that we're obviously focusing on over the next 12 months, and that's throughout the entire product.
more of a development in terms of what people are comfortable AI handling autonomously, and the level of tasks to get more complex.
a big part of what the road map is for the next few months is actually, we don't believe Legal do need to go to summize.com either

kp.k: Validated legal content could support future AI functionality
kp.d: As a more distant possibility, Dunlop discusses using validated templates and advice, potentially sourced from the law-firm community rather than in-house teams, to feed AI. He presents this as an exploratory content direction, not an implemented validation process or evidence that outputs have been verified.
qs: the last one probably is more around a bit further out, but I think there's a lot of interesting concepts on our side to do with content and validation of good content.
whether it be templates, whether it be advice and validated advice, maybe from more of the law firm community than in-house
there can be a bit more of a training guide or more of a validated content that could feed into the AI as well.

kp.k: Voice-driven autonomous contracting remains a future scenario
kp.d: Responding to the host's speculative example of requesting an NDA by voice, Dunlop endorses the possibility of a system that asks follow-up questions and then completes an autonomous process. He anticipates chat and voice becoming major application interfaces and says existing integrations follow that expected direction. He provides no firm implementation date; the host's suggested horizon is not Dunlop's forecast.
qs: we're almost going with that direction and assuming that that's the future of work.

could I see a world where someone essentially does a voice note and says, create an NDA that has these properties and it then goes away and it might ask you some more questions, but ultimately it's an autonomous process. Like very much so, yeah.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dunlop says AI-powered contract workflows reduce routine demand on in-house legal teams, augment lawyers' reviews, and make contract information accessible without a lawyer translating it.
pts.d: Tom Dunlop describes three current Summize use cases: business users create contracts or submit review requests through familiar workplace applications; lawyers use a Microsoft Word add-in for summarization, playbooks, AI assistance, redlining and workflow management; and business users receive natural-language post-signature summaries. He also says generative AI layered over extracted contract data can answer compound questions about renewal dates, notice periods and automatic renewal. These are claims about Summize's combined AI, automation and integration capabilities, not claims that AI alone performs every step. The model combines lawyer augmentation for review with self-service substitution for selected routine interactions.

pts.k: Dunlop claims generative AI improves natural-language contract summaries, but company-specific relevance still requires contextualized data preparation.
pts.d: Dunlop contrasts Summize's earlier pattern recognition, entity extraction and relevance algorithms with its later use of generative AI to turn extracted information into readable summaries. He says AI alone can produce superficially impressive outputs while missing risks specific to a business, such as restrictions affecting a brand-conscious company's IP use. Summize therefore curates and sections information before passing it to a language model. He predicts, cautiously and without a deadline, that generative AI will take on more of this initial complex reasoning. As those capabilities expand, he says summarization is becoming less important as Summize's unique selling proposition relative to its integration of contract touchpoints.

pts.k: Dunlop predicts more complex autonomous contract tasks and conversational interfaces, building on selected workflows he says are already automated.
pts.d: Dunlop reports that some customers already configure NDA creation in Slack to proceed directly to DocuSign and return signed documents to Summize for filing and summarization. This is a described automated workflow, not evidence that the entire process uses agentic reasoning. For the roadmap, he anticipates AI handling more complex tasks autonomously and ultimately allowing a voice request to initiate an NDA workflow, potentially with follow-up questions. He separately predicts lawyers will be able to access nearly all user-facing functionality through Word, Outlook and chat applications rather than visiting Summize's website. He also identifies a more tentative opportunity for validated templates or advice, potentially supplied by the law-firm community, to feed AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Dunlop's experience as an in-house lawyer and vendor founder, descriptions of product architecture, and unnamed customer examples.
pts.d: Dunlop grounds the original problem in his experience spending months manually extracting information from hundreds of contracts during due diligence. He explains how Summize extracts relevant information, uses customer templates or settings to contextualize it, and overlays generative AI. He cites unnamed customers using automated NDA workflows. The interview provides no quantified time or cost savings, accuracy measurements, benchmarks, controlled comparisons or independently documented customer outcomes. Predictions about advanced reasoning, voice interfaces and greater autonomy are presented as expectations and roadmap intentions rather than measured findings. The host's advertising claims are not treated as evidence for Dunlop's claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Dunlop distinguishes current functionality from near-term development and undated longer-term possibilities; autonomy depends on customer comfort and configuration.
pts.d: Dunlop dates the original extraction and summarization work to around 2018. Current claims concern functionality described as available at the interview, including released AI redlining and configured NDA automation. He places increasingly sophisticated AI tasks on an 'over the next 12 months' horizon and expanded native integrations within 'the next few months,' relative to the interview, rather than a specified calendar deadline. Validated-content concepts are 'a bit further out'; voice-driven autonomy and improved initial reasoning have no firm date. The document is labeled 2025, but the discussion also references 2024, so the relative roadmap periods should not be converted into precise dates. Relevant conditions include customer-specific reference material, structured extracted data, use of Summize as the core repository, and willingness to automate selected workflows. Dunlop does not adopt a definite five-year forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are corporate legal teams and their internal business clients; legal-tech vendors and potentially law firms also face changing roles.
pts.d: Dunlop's claims principally concern enterprise contract work. Sales and marketing personnel gain self-service contract creation, submission and information retrieval within their existing applications. In-house lawyers are expected to receive less routine work and conduct remaining reviews more efficiently within Word and Outlook. He does not predict lawyer headcount reductions or wholesale replacement. For Summize as a legal-tech vendor, broader generative-AI capability shifts differentiation away from summarization toward embedded workflows and structured contract data. Law firms appear only as a possible future source of validated content. The interview does not establish an AI-related claim about unmet civil legal need or access to justice.
